meta.title: Indonesian — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 21 letters, vowels and spelling rules — start here, beside UKBI 1
meta.desc: How Indonesian is read and spelled, before or beside the first word: 21 notes, one card each — 7 vowel spellings (a, e, i, o, u, and ai and au at the end of a word), 9 consonant letters and pairs of letters whose sound is not the one an English reader gives them (c, g, h, k, kh, ng, ny, r, v), and 5 rules: where the stress falls, di and ke written apart or joined, the word written twice, how the prefix meng- changes with its root, and -ku, -mu and -nya written onto the word. Indonesian is spelled close to its sound, so the deck is short; what it holds is what the spelling does not tell an English reader. The letter e is three vowels and nothing on the page says which (196 of UKBI 1's 506 headwords contain it, and the e of besar is not the e of enak), c is never k or s (15 headwords), a final k is a glottal stop (23), ng is one sound and ngg is that sound and a g (54 and 10), ny is one sound (7); 258 of the 506 contain at least one of these. The front shows the letters. The back gives the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound it resembles, then words of the UKBI 1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, and the word's own transcription from the dictionary (ˈ stands before the stressed syllable). Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. THE ORDER is the vowels, the consonants, then the rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it is meant to be studied beside UKBI 1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: nothing is written for this deck. Each English comparison is a cell of the first page named below, and each sentence under a letter a sentence of its notes or of the fourth page; the rules are sentences of the second, third and fourth pages, with a cut marked […], and the meanings of -ku, -mu and -nya are the English Wiktionary's. The second row of ng puts that page's cells for ŋ and ɡ side by side, which is what the words' transcriptions show. The letters that sound as an English reader expects (b, d, f, j, l, m, n, p, s, t, w, y) have no card, and neither have sy (the sh of shoe) and z, which no UKBI 1 headword contains. The meng- card shows the changes UKBI 1's own cards show, so it has no example of a root in s. The speaker is your device's Indonesian voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — English comparisons and notes: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Indonesian and Malay”, revision 1334069601 of 2026-01-21. Rules: Wikipedia, “Indonesian orthography”, revision 1384102587 of 2026-11-06; Wikipedia, “Malay phonology”, revision 1379837430 of 2026-10-12; Wikipedia, “Indonesian language”, revision 1385665763 of 2026-11-14 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions and the meanings of -ku, -mu and -nya: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words and meanings: the UKBI 1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: where the stress falls
fields.Says: It is generally the penultimate syllable that is stressed, unless its vowel is a schwa /ə/. If the penult has a schwa, then stress usually moves to the final syllable.
fields.Examples:
as in

empat[əmˈpat̪̚]four

fields.Name: apart, or joined to the word
fields.Says: The writing of di- and ke- (prefixes) can be distinguished from di and ke (prepositions), where di- and ke- are written together with the words that follow them, for example, diambil, kehendak ('taken', 'desire'), while di and ke are written separately from the words that follow them, for example, di rumah, ke pasar ('at home', 'to the market').
fields.Examples:

ke mana[ˌkə ˈma.na]where? (in which direction)
di sinihere; over here

fields.Name: the prefix changes with the root's first sound
fields.Says: Important in the derivation of Malay verbs and nouns is the assimilation of the nasal consonant at the end of the derivational prefixes meng- /məŋ/, a verbal prefix, and peng- /pəŋ/, a nominal prefix. The nasal segment is dropped before sonorant consonants (nasals /m, n, ɲ, ŋ/, liquids /l, r/, and approximants /w, j/). It is retained before and assimilates to obstruent consonants: labial /m/ before labial /p, b/, alveolar /n/ before alveolar /t, d/, post-alveolar /ɲ/ before /tʃ, dʒ/ and /s/, velar /ŋ/ before other sounds (velar /k, ɡ/, glottal /h/, all vowels). In addition, following voiceless obstruents, apart from /tʃ/ (that is /p, t, s, k/), are dropped […].

mendengar[mən.dəˈŋar]hearing (able to hear)
mengambil[məˈŋam.bɪl]to take (in most senses); to take up
